title: Web Scraping Basics
summary: Web scraping is the technique of automatically extracting information from web pages, and it is a valuable automation skill for gathering data that is not available through an API - price monitoring, collecting listings, aggregating news, or building
content:
# Web Scraping Basics ##### The price that moved at midnight A small electronics reseller in Nashik could never work out why their margins kept slipping. Their three main competitors changed prices constantly, and by the time anyone noticed, they had spent a week selling below market or losing sales by sitting above it. The fix was a scraper: a script that visited three public product pages twice a day, extracted the price, and logged it to a sheet with a timestamp. Simple, polite, one request per page. Within a month they had a price history chart and could react in hours instead of weeks. **Web scraping** is the automated extraction of information from web pages. It is a genuinely valuable skill — the internet is full of public data with no API — and it is also the topic where beginners most often get themselves into trouble, legally and technically. So we will treat both halves seriously. ##### Common use cases Scraping earns its place when the data is public, useful, and unavailable in structured form: - **Price and competitor monitoring** — the story above. - **Job or property listings aggregation** across multiple portals. - **Research datasets** — academic papers, government statistics, public records. - **Lead research** — company names and public contact pages from directories. - **Content monitoring** — detecting when a page changes. - **Availability checks** — stock, appointment slots, exam results. Scraping is *not* the right answer when an API exists, when the data is behind a login you do not own, when the terms of service prohibit it, or when the data is personal information you have no legal basis to collect. ##### How HTML is structured To extract data from a page you must understand its shape. HTML is a tree of nested **elements**, each with a tag name, optional **attributes**, and content: ```html

Mechanical Keyboard

₹2,499.00

In stock View details
``` The parts you will target: - **Tag** — `div`, `h3`, `p`, `a`, `span`, `table`, `li`. - **Class** — `class="price"`. Reusable, so many elements share one. This is your most common hook. - **ID** — `id="main"`. Unique on the page, so it is the most precise hook when available. - **Attributes** — `href`, `src`, `data-sku`. Often where the useful value actually lives. Open any page, right-click the value you want, choose **Inspect**, and read the surrounding HTML. That is the entire discovery process. ##### Parsing with BeautifulSoup `requests` fetches the HTML; **BeautifulSoup** turns that text into a navigable tree. ```bash pip install requests beautifulsoup4 lxml ``` ```python import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup resp = requests.get("https://quotes.toscrape.com/", timeout=15) resp.raise_for_status() soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "lxml") # find() returns the first match; find_all() returns a list first = soup.find("div", class_="quote") print(first.find("span", class_="text").get_text(strip=True)) # CSS selectors are usually cleaner for card in soup.select("div.quote"): text = card.select_one("span.text").get_text(strip=True) author = card.select_one("small.author").get_text(strip=True) tags = [t.get_text(strip=True) for t in card.select("a.tag")] print(f"{author}: {text[:50]}... {tags}") ``` The methods you need are few: | Method | Purpose | |---|---| | `soup.find(tag, class_=...)` | First matching element, or `None` | | `soup.find_all(tag, class_=...)` | All matches, as a list | | `soup.select("css selector")` | All matches via CSS — usually most readable | | `soup.select_one("css")` | First CSS match | | `el.get_text(strip=True)` | Visible text, whitespace trimmed | | `el["href"]` / `el.get("href")` | Attribute value (`.get()` is safe) | Two robustness habits, immediately. Use `select_one` and check for `None` before calling `.get_text()` — a missing element is the number one crash. And use `urljoin` for links, because `href="/products/kb-01"` is relative: ```python from urllib.parse import urljoin link_el = card.select_one("a.details") link = urljoin(resp.url, link_el["href"]) if link_el else None ``` ##### requests versus a browser This distinction saves hours of confusion. `requests` fetches the **raw HTML the server sends**. It does not run JavaScript. For a traditional server-rendered site — most blogs, news sites, government portals, e-commerce listing pages — that HTML contains everything, and `requests` + BeautifulSoup is fast, light and perfect. Modern single-page applications (React, Vue, Angular) send a nearly empty HTML shell and then build the page with JavaScript in the browser. Fetch one with `requests` and you get `
` and nothing else. How to tell in ten seconds: run your script, `print(resp.text[:2000])`, and search for a value you can see on the page. Present? Use `requests`. Absent? You have three options, in order of preference: 1. **Find the underlying API.** Open DevTools → Network → XHR, reload, and look for a request returning JSON.
